body.p: Claims 2-20 are pending in the present application, of which claim 2 is an
independent claim. Claims 2, 8, 10, 11 and 13 have been amended herein for clarification.
No new matter is provided by the amendments made herein.
35 U.S.C. 103 Rejections
Claims 2-10 and 13-18 and 20 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being
unpatentable over Willis et al. (U.S. Patent No. 6,216,027) in view of Govari (U.S. Patent
No. 6,716,166) and Foley et al. (U.S. Publication No. 2011/0028894).
It is submitted that Willis, Govari and Foley, alone or in combination, fail to teach
or suggest at least:
2. A catheter system comprising:
a diagnostic catheter comprising:

an elongate shaft comprising a distal end; an expandable assembly mounted to the elongate shaft, the expandable assembly comprising multiple splines and configured to transition from a compacted state to an expanded state;
a plurality of electrodes coupled to the multiple splines of the expandable assembly, each electrode configured to receive electrical signals; and

a plurality of ultrasound transducers coupled to the multiple splines of the expandable assembly; an ablation catheter comprising: an elongate shaft comprising a distal portion; at least one ablation element positioned on the ablation catheter shaft distal portion and configured to deliver energy to tissue; and
a steerable portion configured to be robotically manipulated;

a distance measurement assembly configured to drive the plurality of ultrasound transducers to produce anatomical geometry data, and to generate data representing a distance between each ultrasound transducer of the plurality of ultrasound transducers and a tissue surface orthogonal to each ultrasound transducer;

a processing unit configured to create a three-dimensional anatomical map based on the produced anatomical geometry data, create electrical information based on the received electric signals, and display the electrical information in relation to the three-dimensional anatomical map; and a robotic assembly configured to manipulate the steerable portion of the ablation catheter based on the anatomical geometry data produced by the distance measurement assembly.
According to amended claim 2, a distance measurement assembly is configured to

drive a plurality of ultrasound transducers of diagnostic catheter to produce anatomical geometry data. Further in amended claim 2, a processing unit is configured to create a three-dimensional anatomical map based on the produced anatomical geometry data, create electrical information based on the received electric signals, and display the electrical information in relation to the three-dimensional anatomical map. Further in amended claim 2, a robotic assembly is configured to manipulate the steerable portion of the ablation catheter based on the anatomical geometry data produced by the distance measurement assembly. Therefore, the ablation catheter in claim 2 is manipulated based on the anatomical geometry data generated based on the ultrasound transducers of the diagnostic
catheter.
As noted in the Office Action, Willis fails to teach, suggest or disclose:

a distance measurement assembly configured to drive the plurality of ultrasound transducers to produce anatomical geometry data, and to generate data representing a distance between each ultrasound transducer of the plurality of ultrasound transducers and a tissue surface orthogonal to each ultrasound transducer; a processing unit configured to create a three-dimensional anatomical map based on the produced anatomical geometry data, create electrical information based on the received electric signals, and display the electrical information in relation to the three-dimensional anatomical map; and a robotic assembly configured to manipulate the steerable portion of the ablation catheter based on the anatomical geometry data produced by the distance measurement assembly, as claimed in amended claim 2.
Govari appears to disclose a catheter using a plurality of transducers to generate

distance measurements between the transducers and surface of an endocardial surface and the distance measurements are used to produce a geometrical map. Govari, like Willis, in no way teaches suggests or discloses a processing unit configured to create electrical information based on the received electric signals, and display the electrical information in relation to the three-dimensional anatomical map, as claimed in claim 2. Govari merely
discloses generating a geometrical map based on the distance measurements.
In addition, Govari in no teaches, suggests or discloses that a robotic assembly

configured to manipulate the steerable portion of the ablation catheter based on the anatomical geometry data produced by the distance measurement assembly generated based on the ultrasound transducers of the diagnostic catheter, as claimed. Govari merely discloses the generation of a geometrical map based on distance measurements between the transducers and surface of an endocardial surface. Govari in no way discloses using the
geometrical data to manipulate another catheter.
Foley, like Willis and Govari fails to teach, suggest or disclose a processing unit
configured to create electrical information based on the received electric signals, and display the electrical information in relation to the three-dimensional anatomical map, as
claimed in claim 2.
In addition, Foley appears to disclose a robotic system for inserting a catheter in a

body that is controlled by an operator via a remote controller (see at least [010]-[012], [014]-[015]). Foley appears to disclose that the robotic system can be automatically or semi-automatically manipulated according to the operator's specifications (see [317]). However, Foley in no way teaches, suggests or discloses that a robotic assembly is configured to manipulate the steerable portion of an ablation catheter based on the anatomical geometry data produced by the distance measurement assembly generated based on the ultrasound transducers of the diagnostic catheter, as claimed. Foley merely discloses a robotic device for inserting a catheter into a body. Foley in no way discloses
using the geometrical data generated by one catheter to manipulate a steerable portion of
another catheter.
Therefore, one of ordinary skill in the art could not arrive at the system of amended
claim 2 based on the combination of the cited documents absent the exercise of inventive skill and to do so can only result from impermissible hindsight reconstruction. Even if
combined, the combination of references would not results in the invention as claimed.
Accordingly, since Willis, Govari and Foley fail to teach or suggest these claimed

features, there is no way to combine the references to obtain teaching or suggestion of the claimed features. Further, the differences between the combination of Willis, Govari and Foley, and the present invention as claimed would not have been obvious to one of ordinary
skill in the art at the time the invention was made.
Since Willis, Govari and Foley, taken alone or in combination, fail to teach, suggest
or disclose the present inventions set forth in claim 2, claim 2 and all claims dependent thereon, are believed to be allowable over the combination of the cited references.
Accordingly, reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejections of claim 2 and all claims dependent thereon under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) based on Willis and Foley is respectfully
requested.
Claims 11 and 12 are rejected under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 103(a) as being
unpatentable over Willis et al. (U.S. Patent No. 6,216,027) in view of Govari (U.S. Patent No. 6,716,166) and Foley et al. (U.S. Publication No. 2011/0028894), as applied above,
and further in view of Scharf (U.S. Publication No. 2010/0298690).
Scharf fails to supply the requisite teaching, suggestion or disclosure to overcome
the deficiencies as described above with regard to Willis and Foley.
Accordingly, since Willis, Govari, Foley and Scharf fail to teach or suggest these
claimed features, there is no way to combine the references to obtain teaching or suggestion of the claimed features. Further, the differences between the combination of Willis, Govari,
Foley and Scharf, and the present invention as claimed would not have been obvious to
one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.
Since Willis, Govari, Foley and Scharf, taken alone or in combination, fail to teach,

suggest or disclose the present inventions set forth in claim 2, claims 2, and all claims dependent thereon, are believed to be allowable over the combination of the cited references. Accordingly, reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejections of claims 11-12 and all claims dependent thereon under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) based on Willis, Govari, Foley
and Scharf is respectfully requested.

been obvious to one of ordinary skill in the art at the time the invention was made.
Since Willis, Govari, Foley and Danehorn, taken alone or in combination, fail to

teach, suggest or disclose the present inventions set forth in claim 2, claim 2, and all claims dependent thereon, are believed to be allowable over the combination of the cited references. Accordingly, reconsideration and withdrawal of the rejections of claim 19 and all claims dependent thereon under 35 U.S.C. 103(a) based on Willis, Govari, Foley and
Danehorn is respectfully requested.
Claims 2-20 are rejected on the ground of non-statutory double patenting as being
unpatentable over claims 1-34 of U.S. Patent No.: 10,004,459, in view of Foley et al. (U.S.
Publication No. 2011/0028894).
Claims 2-20 are rejected on the ground of non-statutory double patenting as being
unpatentable over claims 15 and 16 of U.S. Patent No.: 10,667,753, in view of Foley et al.
(U.S. Publication No. 2011/0028894).
As noted above, Foley fails to teach, suggest or disclose the robotic assembly as
claimed. Therefore, reconsideration and removal of the double patenting rejections are
respectfully requested.
